title: Not reconciling
hook: forgiving doesn't require going back to the relationship

segments.voice: Yesterday, the forgiveness project: Fred Luskin's grievance story, told again with a new center. Your line was less hurt. Did the kinder version come out anywhere? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

A few weeks back, this path stood with Esau as he ran. Today, the same meeting, read to the end of the chapter. Jacob, the younger brother, once tricked Esau out of their father's blessing and ran for his life. Now he is coming home, bracing for the worst. And Genesis says: "And Esau ran to meet him, and embraced him, and fell on his neck, and kissed him: and they wept." It sounds like the last scene of a film. But the chapter keeps going. Esau offers to travel on together. Jacob gently says no. And the two brothers take two different roads. Today: not reconciling.
screen: `TWO BROTHERS MEET.` → `AN EMBRACE, AND TEARS.` → `THEN TWO ROADS.`

segments.voice: First, a distinction from the psychology of forgiveness. Everett Worthington, whose five steps we met two days ago, titled one of his books Forgiving and Reconciling, and he treats them as two different things. Forgiving can happen inside one person. Reconciling takes two people, and it needs trust to be rebuilt, which takes behavior over time from both sides. You can do the first alone. You can't do the second alone. Second, back to Genesis. After the embrace, Jacob says his children are young and his flocks are slow, and he'll follow at their pace. Esau goes home to Seir. Jacob goes to Succoth. The text doesn't tell us why Jacob holds back. Some readers hear caution; some hear wisdom; some hear a man who still can't quite believe he's forgiven. What the story does show is an embrace that is real and a distance that stays. Third, an older pair in the same book. When the herdsmen of Abram, as Abraham is still called there, keep quarreling with his nephew Lot's herdsmen, Abram says: "Let there be no strife, I pray thee, between me and thee." And his answer to keeping the peace is space: "separate thyself, I pray thee, from me." Peace, kept by distance. Fourth, why this matters on an ordinary day. Some relationships can be rebuilt, and that can be good. Others shouldn't be, because going back would mean walking into the same harm. Forgiveness, as Worthington describes it, doesn't ask anyone to walk back in. It can be done from across a field.
screen: `FORGIVING AND RECONCILING: TWO THINGS.` · `AN EMBRACE, THEN TWO ROADS.` · `NO STRIFE, AND SEPARATE LAND.` · `NO ONE HAS TO WALK BACK INTO HARM.` · then, large: `FROM A DISTANCE.`

segments.voice: Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind someone you're no longer close to, or don't want to be close to again. Don't bring them nearer. Leave them at a distance, across a wide field, small and far away. From where you sit, let the rope between you go slack. You're not walking over. You're not calling them. You're only letting go of your end. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer from right where you are. The gap stays. The bell holds the time.
Not reconciling. Forgiving can happen inside one person; reconciling takes two and rebuilt trust. You can forgive and still keep the distance. Today's word.
Your line: from a distance. Today, if someone from your past crosses your mind, let go of your end of the rope, and leave the gap exactly where it is. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: Some counselors who work with forgiveness separate it from reconciliation: a person may forgive privately, in writing that is never sent or in prayer, without restoring contact.
